html:
The Glades culture is the name archaeologists give to the peoples of the far south of Florida, around the Everglades and the Florida Keys, from about 500 BCE until contact with Europeans. The map shows it from 500 BCE to 400 CE.

They did not farm. Food came from the water and the swamps: fish, shellfish, turtles and sea mammals, with deer, palm berries and roots. Stone was scarce, so they made tools from shell and bone, and their shell heaps still mark the coast. They also dug canals and built mounds.

The Miami Circle, a ring of holes cut into limestone at the mouth of the Miami River about 2,000 years ago, is one of their best-known sites.

Later peoples of the region came out of this tradition, among them the Tequesta around Miami, the Mayaimi near Lake Okeechobee and, on the west coast, the Calusa, who built a powerful chiefdom without farming.

The Spanish reached Florida in 1513. Disease and slave raids from the north wore these peoples down, and when Spain handed Spanish Florida to Britain in 1763, the last of them left with the Spanish for Cuba.
